claims.text: The initial material is a W–Cu composite with tungsten particles embedded in a copper matrix.
The conventional W–Cu composite has high W–Cu interfacial thermal resistance.
A thin Ti/Ni coating can be deposited on reinforcement particles before composite fabrication.
Depositing a Ti/Ni nanolayer on tungsten particles will produce a stronger metallurgical interface with copper.
A Ti/Ni nanolayer will bridge the thermal mismatch between tungsten and copper.
A Ti/Ni nanolayer will bridge the mechanical mismatch between tungsten and copper.
Improved interfacial bonding from the Ti/Ni coating will reduce W–Cu interfacial thermal resistance.
Reduced interfacial thermal resistance will promote more efficient thermal-energy transfer across the W–Cu boundary.
The interfacial coating will not alter the bulk composition of either the tungsten or copper phase.
The coated W–Cu composite will have higher effective thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable uncoated W–Cu composite.
The coated W–Cu composite will retain mechanical durability comparable to that of the uncoated composite.
The coated W–Cu composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to that of the uncoated composite.
The coating will make W–Cu composites better suited to high-flux, high-radiation fusion-reactor applications.
The proposed effect depends on optimization of the coating thickness and composition.
An excessively thick or reactive coating could compromise mechanical integrity.
An excessively thick or reactive coating could degrade under irradiation.
High thermal flux, irradiation, mechanical loading, and thermal cycling are representative operating conditions for fusion-reactor joints.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires preservation of mechanical durability and irradiation resistance, but the falsification rule is phrased to falsify only when the absence of a conductivity increase occurs without degradation. Under that rule, observed mechanical or irradiation degradation is not itself clearly designated as falsifying, despite contradicting the predicted outcome.
